passage: When a town decides to honour someone or something in public, its first instinct is usually to reach for bronze and stone. Durability is treated as a measure of respect: a statue meant to last for centuries seems to say more than a banner meant to last for a week. Yet the history of public art suggests that permanence is less a virtue than a wager, and frequently a losing one. A monument fixes one generation's judgement in a material that will outlast the judgement itself. Within a few decades the figure on the plinth may be unrecognised by most passers-by, and within a century it may be the cause of a quarrel its makers could not have imagined.

The problem is not that later generations are fickle. It is that a permanent work is designed to end discussion rather than to take part in it. Once installed, it asks only to be accepted; there is no procedure built into it for being reconsidered. When disagreement finally arrives, it therefore arrives as a crisis, with petitions, counter-petitions and arguments over whether removal amounts to erasing history. A city that had expected its public art to change would face no such crisis, because it would already possess a habit of revisiting what stands in its squares.

Temporary works offer one way of building that habit. A plinth that hosts a different commission every year or two, a sculpture placed in a park for a single season, a mural painted on the understanding that it will be painted over: each of these makes public art an occasion rather than a verdict. People argue about the new piece, grow fond of it or feel relieved to see it go, and in doing so they practise exactly the kind of collective judgement that a permanent statue forecloses. The work matters less as an object than as the conversation it starts.

This argument has limits, and they should be stated. Temporary art can slide into novelty for its own sake, a rotating series of spectacles chosen to attract visitors rather than to say anything. And some public works aim at permanence for good reason: a memorial to the dead of a war or a disaster is meant to resist the passing of time, because forgetting is precisely the danger it guards against. The case against bronze is not a case against all lasting memorials. It is a case against the assumption that whatever a public wishes to honour must be honoured in a form that can never be questioned without a fight.

passage: Arguments about the legacy of empire often take the form of an account book. On one side of the ledger are the railways, telegraphs, irrigation canals and universities that colonial governments built; on the other are the drained revenues, the famines, the suppressed industries and the humiliations of foreign rule. Defenders of empire add up the first column and find a surplus; its critics add up the second and find a debt. The exchange can continue indefinitely, because each side chooses what to count, and because neither can say what a fair price for a railway would be.

The deeper difficulty is that the ledger treats the items in the first column as gifts, things handed over to a population that would otherwise have lacked them. Consider the railway. In much of the colonial world, lines were laid out to connect mines, plantations and cotton-growing districts to the ports, and to move soldiers quickly to places where unrest might break out. Routes, gauges and freight rates were set according to the needs of export trade and military control, and the cost of construction was frequently met from local taxation or guaranteed by it. A railway designed in this way is not a present; it is an investment made by one party, with another party's money, for the first party's purposes. To enter it as a credit in the colonised society's account is to confuse being affected by something with being given it.

None of this means that colonial railways were useless to the people who lived alongside them. Passengers, often in numbers that surprised the companies, used the trains to visit distant shrines, to look for work in growing cities, to carry goods to new markets and, eventually, to travel to political meetings that the authorities would have preferred them not to attend. A technology built for one end was turned to others. But this point cuts against the ledger rather than in its favour, since the uses that mattered most to ordinary people were precisely the ones the builders had not intended and could not claim as their contribution.

What the account-book approach leaves out, then, is the question of who decided. A society that chooses to borrow money and build a railway, and gets the routes wrong, has made its own mistake and can learn from it. A society that has a railway built for it, on terms set elsewhere, has acquired a piece of infrastructure but not the habit of deciding about infrastructure. That second loss does not appear in any column, which is perhaps why the ledger has proved so durable: it allows both its defenders and its critics to argue about outcomes while ignoring the matter of agency altogether.

passage: The secret ballot is now so taken for granted that it is easy to forget how recent it is and how fiercely it was once opposed. For much of the nineteenth century, in many countries, voters declared their choices aloud or on papers that others could see, and the reform that replaced this practice was resisted not only by those who profited from intimidation. A respectable strand of liberal opinion held that the vote was a public trust, exercised on behalf of the whole community, and that a trust ought to be discharged in public. A man who knew that his neighbours would see his vote, the argument ran, would be ashamed to cast it for a selfish reason.

The argument has a certain nobility, and it rests on a real insight: people do behave differently when they are observed. Its error lies in assuming that the observer will be the voter's conscience. In practice the people most interested in how a tenant, a labourer or a clerk had voted were the landlord, the employer and the local party agent, and the pressure they applied had little to do with the public good. Publicity did not make votes more responsible; it made them more obedient.

The less obvious virtue of secrecy is that it disarms bribery as well as intimidation. Buying a vote is a kind of contract, and a contract is worthless if one party cannot check whether the other has kept it. Once no one can verify how a ballot was marked, the buyer who pays in advance cannot know whether he has bought anything, and the seller can take the money and vote as he pleases. Secrecy, in other words, works less by appealing to the voter's virtue than by making a certain kind of corruption unenforceable. This also explains why secrecy has to be a duty and not merely a right. If voters could choose to reveal their ballots, those under pressure could be required to prove their compliance, and the protection would collapse for exactly the people who need it most.

That point matters more now than it once did. A ballot marked at home, at a kitchen table, can be watched by a domineering relative; a ballot photographed in a booth with a telephone can be shown to whoever demands proof. Neither practice is sinister in itself, and both make voting easier for many people. But they reopen the gap that secrecy was designed to close, and they suggest that the privacy of the vote is not a natural condition of democratic life but an arrangement that has to be maintained, and occasionally rebuilt, as the means of voting change.

passage: When a job that was once filled by school leavers begins to advertise for graduates, the usual explanation is that the work has become more demanding. Machines have taken over the routine tasks, the story goes, and what remains calls for the analytical habits that only a university can supply. There is something to this. Some occupations really have changed beyond recognition, and an office clerk today handles systems that would have baffled a clerk of fifty years ago. But the explanation is offered far more often than it is checked, and when one looks at what people in many of these jobs actually do, the change in the work is often modest beside the change in the paperwork required to get it.

A more economical account treats the degree less as a certificate of skill than as a ticket in a queue. When few people held degrees, an employer who asked for one was selecting a small group who were, on average, more persistent and better connected than the rest. As degrees became common, the same requirement no longer separated anyone, and employers who wanted to keep selecting raised the bar again, asking for a master's where a bachelor's had once sufficed. Each employer is behaving sensibly; it is merely using the cheapest filter available. Yet the sum of these sensible choices resembles a crowd at a parade in which everyone stands on tiptoe: no one sees better than before, and everyone is more tired.

The costs of this arrangement are not evenly spread. Students from families that can afford several years of fees and forgone earnings keep pace with the rising bar; those who cannot are shut out of work they could perfectly well perform. A requirement introduced in the name of competence thus ends up rewarding the capacity to pay for time. Meanwhile the graduates themselves often discover that much of what they studied is barely used in the job, and that what the employer valued was the signal rather than the substance.

None of this is an argument against education, which has goods that no labour market can measure. It is an argument against confusing two things that the word 'qualification' runs together: what a person can do, and how long a person has been able to stay in school. Some employers have begun to test applicants directly on the tasks the job involves. Where this is done, an awkward question comes into view, namely whether the degree requirement it replaces was ever a guarantee of quality or merely a habit that nobody had thought to examine.

passage: Income is the most convenient measure of how well people are doing, and convenience has a way of turning into authority. A figure for income per head can be compared across countries and decades, added up and divided, and reported to a decimal place. Yet what it measures is a means. People do not value income for its own sake but for what it allows them to do and to be: to be adequately nourished, to move about without danger, to read, to take part in the life of a community, to have some say in the decisions that shape their lives. The capability approach, as it has come to be called, proposes that development should be judged by these freedoms directly rather than by the resources that are supposed to produce them.

The case for the shift rests on a simple observation with large consequences. The same income does not yield the same freedoms to everyone. A person who uses a wheelchair needs more resources than a neighbour to reach the same workplace; a pregnant woman needs more food than a man of the same age to be equally well nourished; a household in a cold climate must spend on heating what a household elsewhere can spend on anything it likes. Social arrangements matter as much as bodies and climates. Where custom keeps women from travelling alone, a rise in household income may leave a daughter's freedom to attend a distant college exactly where it was. Measures of income, by construction, are blind to these differences in the rate at which resources become lives.

The standard objection is that the approach, whatever its philosophical appeal, cannot be made to work. Which capabilities count? How should being literate be weighed against being healthy, or political voice against freedom from hunger? Any answer, critics say, is either so vague as to be useless or, once written down as a definite list with definite weights, an imposition of some theorist's values on people who might rank their lives differently. A list drawn up in a university, they add, need not be the list that a farmer or a factory worker would draw up, and a framework that began by taking people's own lives seriously would then end by overruling their judgments about those lives.

The objection is weaker than it looks, because it applies with equal force to the measure it is meant to defend. Income per head also aggregates very different things, and it also weights them. It weights them by market prices, which record what people with money are willing to pay, so that a luxury bought by the rich can count for more than a staple that the poor cannot afford. These are value judgments as well; they are simply made silently, by the market, rather than openly, by someone who must defend them. A framework that forces its users to state and argue for their weights has not introduced a new difficulty. It has exposed an old one.

This does not mean that every attempt to turn capabilities into a single index succeeds. Composite scores that average a few indicators can reproduce the very problem the approach set out to solve, burying under one number the differences in conversion that made income misleading in the first place. The approach is at its strongest not as a rival ranking but as a discipline of attention: a way of asking, in any given place, which freedoms people lack and why, and of noticing when a rising average conceals a stagnant life.

passage: Conservation has always had favourites. Appeals for money are illustrated with tigers, pandas, whales and elephants, animals with large eyes, recognisable faces and a reputation for grandeur, and rarely with a beetle, a freshwater mussel or a lichen. Critics have long complained that this distorts priorities. If donors give to what they find beautiful, the argument runs, then most of the living world, which is small, drab or simply invisible, will be neglected, and the species most in need of help will be the least likely to receive it. The objection is not merely aesthetic. Insects, fungi and the small organisms of soil and water do much of the work that keeps ecosystems running, yet they attract only a tiny share of public concern.

The complaint has force, but it is weaker than it first appears, because a charismatic animal rarely receives protection on its own. A large predator needs a large area, and the forest or grassland that is protected for its sake also shelters thousands of less appealing species that no donor would have paid to save directly. In this sense the famous animal works as a kind of advertisement for an entire landscape. The money is raised in the name of one face, but it is spent, at least in part, on soil, water and cover that serve everything living there.

The defence holds only up to a point, however. Some of the most threatened organisms live in habitats that no charismatic animal shares: a single cave, a spring, a patch of chalk grassland, the gravel bed of one river. Protecting a tiger reserve will do nothing for them. Moreover, money given in the name of a famous animal is sometimes spent on that animal directly, on breeding programmes, tracking collars or patrols against poachers, rather than on the wider habitat, and in such cases the advertising argument does not apply at all. A donor who pays for a radio collar has helped one tiger, and perhaps the scientists who follow it, but not the river below the reserve.

The sensible conclusion is neither to abandon flagship species nor to treat them as a complete strategy. They are a tool for raising attention and money, and a useful one. But a conservation movement that allowed the tastes of donors to draw its map of priorities would leave large gaps, and those gaps would fall precisely where the most unfamiliar forms of life are found. Some part of the effort has to be directed by need rather than by appeal, even when need comes in the shape of a mussel.

passage: Cuteness is usually treated as the least serious of aesthetic qualities, if it is admitted to be an aesthetic quality at all. It belongs, we suppose, to stickers, toys and advertisements, and a taste for it is regarded as something to grow out of. Yet this dismissal sits oddly with the sheer power of the response. Few experiences in the visual world are as immediate or as hard to resist as the one produced by a large-eyed, round-faced, short-limbed creature stumbling towards us; we feel it before we have decided anything, and it is remarkably similar across cultures that agree on little else in matters of taste.

Students of animal behaviour noticed long ago that the features we find cute, a large head relative to the body, big low-set eyes, softness and clumsiness, are the features of the very young, and they proposed that the response is a mechanism for securing care. The explanation is plausible, but it accounts for less than it seems to. It tells us why infants elicit tenderness; it does not tell us why we find the same tenderness stirred by a cartoon kettle with eyes, or why the response is so readily extended to objects that need no care whatever. Once detached from the infant, the cute becomes a style, and a style can be applied to anything.

What makes the style interesting is its ambivalence. The cute object presents itself as small, soft and unable to resist, and our response to it is mixed in a way that tenderness towards a real child usually is not. Alongside the wish to protect, there is often a wish to possess and to handle, the half-joking urge to squeeze or pinch what one finds adorable, which people frequently admit to with some embarrassment. The cute flatters our power as much as it summons our care: it is an image of something that will never answer back.

This is why cuteness should be taken seriously rather than either indulged or sneered at. A quality that disarms judgement so quickly is a useful instrument for anyone who wishes to make something appear harmless, whether a product, an institution or a mascot standing in for an organisation whose activities are anything but soft. None of this means that delight in a kitten is a moral failing, and the pleasure is, in most of its forms, innocent enough. But an aesthetic that works by making us feel strong and kindly at once, and that does so before thought has begun, is not trivial; its very lightness is what gives it weight.

passage: The case for monitoring employees at work usually rests on two claims. The first is that the employer is paying for the worker's time and is therefore entitled to know how that time is spent. The second is that the worker has agreed to the arrangement: the monitoring policy was set out in the contract, and nobody was forced to sign it. Both claims sound reasonable, and both, I think, prove much less than their defenders suppose.

Take the argument from payment first. An employer buys a worker's labour, not the worker; the wage secures a certain kind of effort over a certain period, and it has never been understood to include a right to observe everything a person does while that effort is being given. A firm that pays a carpenter by the day may inspect the cabinets she builds, but it does not thereby acquire a claim to read her letters during lunch. The argument from consent fares little better. Agreement given by someone who needs the job, in a market where most comparable employers impose similar terms, tells us that the terms were accepted, not that they were fair. Consent of this kind can settle a dispute about what was agreed; it cannot settle whether the agreement should have been offered.

The deeper difficulty is what continuous monitoring does to work itself. When every keystroke and pause is recorded, the employee learns to perform for the record rather than for the task. A support worker whose calls are timed will cut short a conversation with a confused customer even when a longer one would solve the problem; an office worker whose idle minutes are logged will keep the screen busy instead of stopping to think. The record begins to replace the judgement it was supposed to check, and the trust on which most skilled work depends, the expectation that a person will use discretion well when no one is looking, quietly erodes. There is an irony here as well: the information that monitoring yields grows less useful the more thoroughly it is collected, because what it captures is increasingly a display staged for the watcher.

None of this means that employers may never watch. The test I would propose is therefore not whether monitoring was agreed to, but whether it is tied to an identifiable hazard and limited to what that hazard requires. General surveillance, justified only by the employer's wish to know, fails that test, however clearly it has been written into the contract.

passage: There is an old argument, revived by students of public finance, that the way a state raises its money shapes the kind of state it becomes. A government that depends on taxing its own population must, to some degree, negotiate with that population. It needs to know who earns what and where they live; it needs officials who can assess, collect and keep accounts; and it needs taxpayers who will comply without being coerced at every turn. Each of these needs creates leverage for the governed. Those who pay can demand to know how their money is spent, and rulers who want a steady revenue have reason to listen.

A government that draws most of its income from a single lucrative resource, such as oil or minerals sold abroad, faces no comparable pressure. Its revenue arrives through a handful of contracts with foreign buyers and requires little cooperation from ordinary citizens. It has no need to build an apparatus that knows the population in detail, and no need to trade services or a voice in decisions for compliance. Proponents of the argument suggest that such states can afford to be both unresponsive and administratively thin, buying acquiescence with subsidies and public employment rather than earning consent through bargaining.

Stated baldly, the thesis is too mechanical. Taxation has often been extracted by force rather than negotiated, and many heavily taxed populations have obtained neither representation nor accountability in return. Nor are all resource-rich states alike: where competent institutions and habits of public scrutiny were established before a windfall arrived, the revenue has sometimes been managed with considerable openness. The sequence appears to matter as much as the source. A resource boom that lands on a weak state may keep it weak; one that lands on a state already accustomed to accounting for itself need not.

What survives these qualifications is a narrower but sturdier claim. The point is not that taxes make governments good or that resource revenue makes them bad, but that accountability tends to grow where rulers need something from the ruled that cannot simply be seized. Taxation is one common source of that need, perhaps historically the most important, but it is the dependence, not the tax form as such, that does the work. A reform that raised more revenue from citizens without increasing what citizens could demand in return would therefore miss the point entirely, and might even entrench the habits of command it was meant to cure. Equally, a resource-rich government that chose to make itself dependent on its citizens, by funding services through broad taxes and setting its windfall aside, would be doing something more significant than balancing its books.

passage: National income statistics were designed to answer a question about production: how much an economy produces in a year. They were never meant to measure welfare, and some of those who built them said as much. But a statistic that is published every quarter, reported on the evening news and used to judge governments acquires a meaning beyond its design. Growth in gross domestic product has come to stand for success, and the blind spots of the measure have come to matter accordingly.

One blind spot bears directly on the environment. When a country fells a forest and sells the timber, the sale counts as production, and nothing is subtracted for the forest that is no longer there. When a country pumps oil from its fields, the revenue counts as income, though the oil in the ground was an asset and its extraction leaves the country with less of it. A household that sold a piece of its furniture every year and described the proceeds as salary would be judged to have misunderstood its own finances. National accounts already make a version of the necessary correction for machines and buildings, deducting their wear to arrive at net product; the same logic, applied consistently, would deduct the depletion of forests, fisheries, minerals and soil.

A second blind spot runs in the opposite direction. Spending that merely repairs damage counts as output. If a factory pollutes a river and the town downstream builds a treatment plant to make the water drinkable again, both the factory's production and the plant's construction add to GDP, though the town ends up with no more clean water than it had before the factory arrived. Defensive spending of this kind can make a deteriorating situation look like growth.

It does not follow that GDP should be abandoned, as some of its critics urge. For the purposes it was designed to serve, such as tracking output and employment through booms and slumps, it remains indispensable, and no alternative matches its consistency across countries and decades. Nor are the corrections straightforward. Valuing the depletion of a fishery requires assumptions about future prices and about the rate at which the stock regenerates, and different assumptions yield very different answers. The more modest and more defensible proposal is to publish, alongside GDP, accounts that record changes in natural assets, so that a country that grows by drawing down its capital can at least be seen to be doing so. A figure that is imperfect but visible is likelier to change behaviour than a correct one that nobody computes.

passage: For a time it was widely believed, among journalists and fact-checkers as much as among researchers, that correcting a false belief could make matters worse. The idea, which came to be called the backfire effect, held that people confronted with evidence against a cherished belief would not merely resist it but cling to the belief more tightly, as though the correction were an attack to be repelled. It had an intuitive appeal: most of us have argued with someone who seemed to grow more certain with every fact we offered. And it carried a discouraging moral. If correction backfires, perhaps it is better not to correct at all.

Subsequent research has been considerably kinder to correction. Larger studies, with more varied topics and more diverse participants, have generally found that people who receive a factual correction move, on average, towards the accurate view, even when the correction cuts against their political loyalties. Reversal of the kind the early findings described appears to be rare, and some of the original results have proved difficult to reproduce. The more careful conclusion is not that people are perfectly responsive to evidence but that they are responsive to it in the ordinary, imperfect way: they update, though often less than they should.

It is worth asking why the backfire idea spread so far on so slender a basis. Part of the answer is that it flattered a certain cynicism about the public, and part is that it confused resistance with reversal. Someone who hears a correction and does not change his mind has resisted it; someone who becomes more convinced of the falsehood has reversed. The first is common and unremarkable, since people rarely abandon a belief after a single encounter with contrary evidence. Only the second would justify the conclusion that correcting is counterproductive, and it is the second that the evidence has failed to find with any regularity.

This does not mean that correction is a cure. Its effects often fade over weeks, so that people drift back towards the belief they were talked out of, and accepting that a particular claim is false does not necessarily change the attitudes the claim was used to support. A voter may concede that a politician's statistic was wrong and still admire the politician exactly as much. These are serious limits, but they are limits of a different kind. They call for corrections that are repeated, that offer an alternative explanation rather than a bare denial, and that are not expected to carry more weight than a single fact can bear. They do not call for silence.

The history of the backfire effect is thus a small lesson about the life of findings as well as about belief. A striking result, especially one that confirms what people already suspect, can travel much faster than the slower work of checking it, and the effort to correct a mistaken finding meets the same ordinary resistance, though not reversal, that greets any correction.

passage: Conservationists have long sorted species into two kinds. Native species belong where they are found and deserve protection; alien species, carried by people beyond their former range, are suspect, and those that spread are labelled invasive and targeted for control. The distinction is so familiar that it is rarely examined, yet it rests on a choice that is not itself ecological. To call a species native is to say that it was present before some date, usually the arrival of a particular wave of human travel or trade, and the date is a convention. Species have always moved, carried by winds, currents and birds or on their own legs, and as the climate warms many are shifting their ranges without any human hand to carry them. A plant that crosses a mountain range by itself is not usually called an invader; one that crosses in a shipment of grain is.

A growing number of ecologists conclude that origin should simply be dropped as a criterion. What matters, they argue, is what a species does. Many introduced species cause no measurable harm, and some are positively useful: they hold soil on eroded slopes, feed pollinators where native flowers have been lost, or provide cover for native birds in landscapes that offer little else. Campaigns to remove such species spend scarce money and can do damage of their own, through herbicides, through disturbance of the ground, or by stripping out shelter on which native animals had come to depend. Judging species by their passports rather than by their effects is, on this view, a kind of ecological nativism, and conservation would do better without it.

The critics are right that origin is not itself a harm, and right that much eradication has been undertaken without asking whether the target was doing any damage. But their alternative assumes that effects can be known at the moment a decision has to be made, and this is often false. Introduced species frequently remain scarce and inconspicuous for decades before something, a change in climate, a new road, the arrival of a suitable pollinator, allows them to spread rapidly. By the time the harm is plain, removal has usually become impossible. Moreover, a newly arrived species has no shared history with the predators, parasites and competitors of its new home, and so its future behaviour there is harder to forecast than that of a species whose relationships have been worked out over a long time. This does not make the newcomer more likely to be harmful; it makes its effects less predictable, which is a different thing.

Seen this way, origin is neither a verdict nor an irrelevance but a piece of evidence, and what it is evidence of is uncertainty. Its weight changes with time. When a species has only just arrived, removal is cheap and its effects are unknown, and a presumption against it is reasonable precisely because the decision cannot wait for the evidence that the critics demand. When a species has been established for a century and its effects can be observed, the presumption has done its work, and the case for removing it should rest on what it is shown to do; the label alien then adds little. Both the defenders of the old distinction and its critics treat the question as one of identity, of what a species is. It is better understood as a question of timing and of knowledge: of what can be known about a species, and when.

passage: The case for deciding by majority is usually made on grounds of fairness rather than wisdom. Majorities are not reliably right, but a procedure that counts each vote equally treats each voter as an equal, and no rival procedure seems to do so as well. There is a second, less often stated part of the case. Majority rule is tolerable to those who lose because losing is expected to be temporary. Today's minority may be tomorrow's majority, since coalitions shift as issues change, and a citizen who is outvoted on one question can reasonably expect to be on the winning side of another. Over time, the losses are spread around.

This second condition does not always hold. When the issues that matter most to people line up with a stable division in the society, by language, region or ancestry, for instance, the same group may find itself outvoted on question after question for generations. Its members cast their votes, and their votes are counted equally, but the counting never changes the result. Formal equality at the ballot box then coexists with something very like permanent exclusion. To tell such a minority that it has been treated fairly because each of its votes weighed as much as anyone else's is to mistake the form of fairness for its substance.

Various remedies have been proposed: requirements of supermajorities for certain decisions, the devolution of some powers to regions where the minority is concentrated, electoral systems that give smaller groups a share of seats, and constitutional rights that no majority may override. Each has costs. Supermajority rules protect minorities by making change difficult, which also protects whatever injustices the status quo contains. Devolution can create new minorities within the regions it empowers. Entrenched rights shift power from elected bodies to courts, whose members the minority usually has no means of holding to account.

None of these costs settles the matter, but together they suggest that the problem should be framed differently. The persistent minority is not evidence that majority rule is unjust in itself. It is evidence that one of the conditions under which majority rule is fair has failed. The aim of a remedy, accordingly, should be to restore that condition where possible, for example by encouraging cross-cutting associations that loosen the grip of a single division on political life, rather than to replace majority rule with a different principle of decision. Where the condition cannot be restored, stronger protections may be needed, but they should be understood as repairs to a damaged procedure, not as a rival theory of legitimacy.

passage: A curious reversal has taken place in the market for handmade goods. For most of history, the aim of a skilled potter or weaver was regularity: bowls that stacked, threads of even thickness, a pattern that repeated without drift. Irregularity was the mark of an apprentice or of a hurried job, and the master's pride lay in eliminating it. Today, by contrast, the small wobble in a glaze or the slight lean of a hand-thrown cup is what many buyers are paying for. It has become the proof that a person, and not a machine, was involved.

The trouble with this proof is that it can be forged. A machine that can make a perfect cup can be programmed to make an imperfect one, and to vary the imperfection from piece to piece so that no two look alike. Tableware with deliberately uneven rims and glazes is already produced in quantity, and an ordinary buyer cannot tell it from the real thing. If what we value in the handmade is irregularity as such, then the handmade has no defence against its imitation, and the premium paid for it is a premium paid for a story.

But irregularity was never the point, and treating it as the point misunderstands what a craftsperson does. A turner working a piece of wood meets a knot, a change in the grain, a softer patch, and alters the cut to suit it; a weaver feels the tension of the warp change with the damp in the air and corrects for it. The handmade object is the record of many such small judgements, each a response to the particular material in front of the maker. Its variations, where they occur, are traces of that responsiveness, not ornaments added afterwards. A machine-made irregularity, however convincing, responds to nothing; it is a pattern generated in advance and imposed on material treated as uniform.

This distinction can be pressed too far. Machines can be built to sense and respond to their material, and a good deal of hand production is as mechanical as anything in a factory, the same motion repeated on identical parts without a thought. The line between craft and its imitation, then, is not drawn by the presence of a hand. It is drawn by whether the making involved attention to the particular, and by that test some machine work would count as craft while much of what is sold as handmade would not.

passage: It is often said that the orderly queue reveals something about a people's character, as if patience were a national trait passed down with the language. The explanation is flattering to those who queue well and insulting to those who do not, and it is mostly wrong. A queue is better understood as a small institution: a shared rule, first come first served, enforced by no official and sustained by people who mostly do not know one another and will never meet again. What needs explaining, therefore, is not why some nations are supposedly virtuous but why such a rule, lacking any formal sanction, holds at all among strangers.

Part of the answer is that the queue makes its own rule visible. Everyone can see the line, everyone can see their place in it, and anyone who pushes in is caught in the act before an audience that has every reason to object. The penalty is rarely more than a sharp word or a collective stare, yet it is usually enough, because the offender cannot pretend not to know the rule. Compare a crowd waiting at the doors of a bus, where no line has formed. Here the same people who would wait patiently at a ticket counter will often jostle, not because they have become selfish but because no one can say with confidence who arrived first. Without a visible order there is nothing to defend and no clear offence to resent.

This suggests that the strength of an informal norm depends less on the virtue of those who follow it than on how legible it makes compliance and violation. Managers of busy offices seem to have grasped this when they introduced numbered tickets: the ticket does not change anyone's character, but it turns an ambiguous crowd into an order that each person can check. Railings, painted footprints and single winding lines that feed many counters work in the same way. The same logic explains why a queue that winds around a corner, so that newcomers cannot tell where it ends, tends to generate precisely the disputes that a visible line prevents. Such devices are inexpensive, and they succeed by removing doubt rather than by threatening punishment.

None of this means that the queue is the fairest possible way to allocate a scarce service. It rewards those with time to spare and ignores urgency; a hospital that treated patients strictly in order of arrival would be orderly and indefensible. Nor should the absence of lines be read as disorder, since a crowd may follow subtler conventions that an outsider fails to notice. The point is narrower. Where people do accept first come first served, the rule survives among strangers because it can be seen, and it falters where it cannot.

passage: In the last two decades the walkable neighbourhood has become one of the few planning ideals on which almost everyone claims to agree, and with agreement has come measurement. Composite indices now rate districts by the number of shops, schools and stops within a short radius, the density of street intersections and the share of homes near public transport. Estate agents quote such figures; municipal plans set targets for raising them. It would be churlish to deny the good these indices have done. They gave walking, long treated as what people did when they could not drive, a place in the arithmetic of planning, and they made visible how many districts had been designed as if nobody would ever arrive on foot.

Yet what the indices measure is proximity, and proximity is not the same as walkability. A street can lie within five minutes of a pharmacy, a school and a bus stop and still be miserable to walk along: a narrow pavement beside four lanes of fast traffic, no shade under a summer sun, the blank walls of parking structures on either side, crossings that demand a long detour. Two districts with identical scores can therefore offer entirely different experiences, and the index has no way of registering the difference, because it counts what lies at the end of the walk and ignores the walk itself.

This blindness is not accidental; it reflects an assumption that walking is chiefly a means of reaching places. For many people it is that, but it is also something more: the way a child learns a neighbourhood, the way an elderly resident keeps in contact with the world, the occasion for the chance encounters on which local life depends. These goods are produced en route, by the quality of the street, its pace, its frontages, its benches and its shade, not by the count of destinations. A measure built around destinations will systematically undervalue them.

The danger is sharpest when the index ceases to be a description and becomes a target. A city told to raise its score can do so cheaply by permitting a few more shops near existing homes, while the hostile road that separates residents from those shops remains untouched. The number improves; the walk does not. None of this argues for abandoning measurement. It argues for remembering what the measurement leaves out, and for treating a high score as the beginning of an inquiry into a street rather than its conclusion.

passage: For anyone who thinks of natural selection as a relentless editor of waste, the tail of a peacock is an embarrassment, since it is heavy, conspicuous and awkward in flight, and it makes its bearer easier for predators to spot and harder for him to escape. Darwin treated such ornaments as a problem of their own, and proposed that they spread not because they helped their owners survive but because they helped them mate: females preferred them, and the preference was enough to carry the trait forward. That answer, however, raised a second and more awkward question, namely why females should come to prefer an ornament that makes their mates less likely to survive.

One influential reply turns the embarrassment into the explanation. An ornament can work as an honest signal precisely because it is costly. A male in poor condition cannot afford to grow and carry an extravagant tail; only a male with ample reserves, and perhaps with sound inherited qualities, can bear the burden and still thrive. A female who chooses the most lavish display is therefore choosing, without knowing it, the male best able to pay. On this view the cost is not a side effect to be minimised but the very thing that keeps the signal reliable. A cheap signal could be produced by anyone, and a signal that anyone can produce soon carries no information.

The idea has been extended well beyond courtship. Some antelope, on spotting a predator, leap high into the air on stiff legs instead of fleeing at once, which looks like a waste of precious seconds. If the leap advertises that the animal is fit enough to outrun any chase, a predator that heeds it saves itself a fruitless pursuit, and the leaper is spared an attack. Here too, the display persuades because it could not be produced by an animal that lacked the quality it advertises.

It would be a mistake, though, to treat costliness as the whole story. Theoretical work suggests that what matters is not that a signal is expensive in absolute terms but that it is more expensive for weak individuals than for strong ones; a signal equally costly for all would sort no one. Nor need every ornament be honest. Some preferences may persist simply because females who hold them have sons who inherit the admired trait, a self-reinforcing loop that can carry ornaments well beyond any useful information. The costly signal, in short, explains why many displays can be trusted, not why every display exists.

passage: A parent who hears a child begin a sentence in one language and finish it in another often worries that the child has learned neither properly. Teachers have voiced the same anxiety, and so, at times, have bilingual speakers themselves, who describe their own mixing with a kind of apology, as though it betrayed a laziness they ought to overcome. The assumption behind the worry is simple: a speaker who switches must be reaching for a word he does not have, and a speaker who is constantly reaching has not finished learning.

The assumption is not absurd, and sometimes it is true. Anyone who has lived between two languages knows the moment when the word for a kitchen utensil, or for a form at the bank, has been acquired in one language and simply not in the other. But careful recordings of bilingual conversation suggest that such gaps account for only part of what happens, and not the most interesting part. Switches tend to fall at points where the grammars of the two languages fit together and to avoid points where they clash, so that a sentence begun in one language and finished in another is usually well formed by the standards of both. A speaker who was merely groping for words would not be so tidy. To switch in this way, one needs to know two grammars well enough to sense, without thinking, where they can be joined.

Nor is the timing of a switch random. Speakers move into the other language to report what someone else said, to mark a change of topic, to soften a refusal, to signal that a remark is a joke, or to draw a listener in or shut one out. A grandmother's proverb may be quoted in the language she used, not because the speaker cannot translate it, but because the translation would lose the grandmother. In such uses the switch itself carries meaning, much as a change of tone does within a single language; it is a resource that monolingual speakers lack, not a failure that they have avoided.

None of this means that every setting must welcome mixing. An examination set in one language, or a document that must be read by people who know only one, may reasonably require a speaker to stay within it, and a bilingual who could not do so would indeed have a problem. The error lies in treating the ability to keep languages apart as the measure of competence, and the habit of combining them as its absence. Most bilinguals can do both. Judging them by the first alone is like judging a pianist only by whether she can play with one hand.

passage: In ordinary speech leisure is what is left over when work is done. It is time off, and its value is usually explained by reference to the work it interrupts: we rest so that we can return refreshed, and an employer who grants generous holidays is said to be investing in productivity. Even our defences of free time tend to be framed in these terms. Leisure, on this picture, is the pause that makes the next effort possible, and a person who takes too much of it is quietly suspected of having failed at something.

Aristotle saw the relation the other way round. In the Nicomachean Ethics he argues that we are busy in order to have leisure, much as we make war in order to have peace, and the Greek word for leisure, schole, is the ancestor of our word 'school'. Leisure in his sense was not rest or idleness. It was the condition of being free to engage in activities chosen for their own sake, of which he held contemplation to be the highest, though he also counted the cultivated enjoyment of music among its proper occupations. Amusement, by contrast, belonged with work. We need relaxation because we cannot labour continuously, and amusement provides it, so amusement exists for the sake of further activity rather than as an end in itself; to toil for the sake of amusement struck him as childish.

The modern inversion has a consequence that is easy to miss. Once leisure is understood as recovery for the sake of work, it inherits the standards of work. Free time becomes something to be used well, which increasingly means used productively: hobbies are pursued for the skills they build, exercise for the stamina it sustains, even sleep for its effect on the next day's performance. The result is not merely that people have too little time off, though many do, but that the time they have is colonised by the logic it was supposed to interrupt. Aristotle would have recognised the pattern. A life organised entirely around work and the recovery it requires has, in his terms, no leisure at all, however many holidays it contains.

The obvious objection is that Aristotle's leisure was a privilege resting on the labour of others. The citizens free for philosophy and politics were supported by slaves, by women whose sphere he confined to the household, and by labourers and artisans whom he considered unsuited to full citizenship in the best city. A conception of the good life that excludes most people from it can hardly serve as a model for a society in which nearly everyone must work. This objection is just, and it should not be softened. But it tells against the distribution of leisure in Aristotle's city, not against his account of what leisure is. One can reject the arrangement that gave a few men freedom from necessity while still holding that freedom from necessity is valuable for what it makes possible, and that what it makes possible is not simply more work.

What follows for us is less a programme than a question. If the value of leisure lies in activities worth doing for their own sake, then the measure of a society's free time is not only how much of it there is but whether people have the means, the education and the settled habits to fill it with such activities, rather than with recovery alone. That is a demand on schools and cities as much as on employers, and it is one that the language of rest and productivity has no words to state.

passage: Few words in the vocabulary of management carry as much reproach as slack. Idle machines, unfilled hours, inventory sitting in warehouses and staff whose days are not fully booked all appear, to the analyst armed with a spreadsheet, as resources that are paid for and not used. The programmes that set out to remove them, under whatever name is fashionable at the time, can usually point to impressive savings in their first year, and the savings are real. What such programmes measure less well is what the slack had been doing before it was removed, because its work was done in circumstances that the measurements were not designed to capture.

The first of those circumstances is the shock. A supply chain that holds no spare stock is cheaper to run on every ordinary day, and on the day a single supplier fails it halts entirely, because there is nothing between the failure and the factory floor. A hospital ward staffed exactly to its average occupancy works smoothly in most weeks and is overwhelmed in the week that an infection spreads. In each case the margin that looked like waste was a store of capacity held against an event whose timing could not be known, and its value appears only in the period that the efficiency audit treats as an exception. To judge slack by ordinary days is to judge an umbrella by the weather on days when it did not rain.

The second circumstance is less dramatic and perhaps more important. Organisations do not only respond to events; they also change themselves, and change requires time that is not already claimed. An engineer who has an afternoon free may try out an idea that no plan had scheduled; a manager with some unallocated budget can fund a small experiment without first writing a case for it that no one yet knows how to write. Most of these experiments come to nothing, which is exactly why a system that requires every hour and every rupee to be justified in advance will not permit them. The new products and methods that later look inevitable often began in precisely the margins that a thorough efficiency drive would have closed.

It would be naive to conclude that slack is always benign. Spare resources can shelter inefficiency as easily as invention, and a department with more staff than it needs may use the surplus not to experiment but to protect its own comfort or to fight for its standing within the firm. Some slack is indeed waste, and some of the people who defend it are defending their privileges. The critics of slack are therefore not simply wrong; they are answering a question that is badly posed. Asking how much slack an organisation has, and how quickly it can be reduced, treats a heterogeneous quantity as if it were uniform.

The more useful question is what the slack is for and who can see it. A reserve whose purpose is understood, whose size is reviewed and whose use is reported can be defended on the days when it seems idle, and trimmed when it has outlived its purpose. A reserve that exists only because no one has looked at it will be either preserved for the wrong reasons or eliminated by the first auditor who does. The aim is neither to maximise slack nor to abolish it, but to hold it deliberately, as an organisation holds any other asset whose returns arrive irregularly.
